# Summary: Autoencoder
An **autoencoder** is a neural network architecture comprised of an encoder function ( E_\phi: \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{Z} ) and a decoder function ( D_\theta: \mathcal{Z} \to \mathcal{X} ) , typically mapping from a higher-dimensional input space ( \mathbb{R}^m ) to a lower-dimensional latent space ( \mathbb{R}^n ) (with ( m > n ) ) and back. The encoder compresses input data into a latent representation (code), while the decoder reconstructs the input from this code. Autoencoders are trained to minimize a reconstruction loss, often mean squared error, over a data distribution or empirical dataset.
To prevent trivial copying, undercomplete autoencoders constrain the latent dimension to be smaller than the input, thus encouraging meaningful feature extraction and data compression. Extensions include variational autoencoders (VAEs), which model the latent space probabilistically, sparse autoencoders that enforce sparsity on the latent code, denoising autoencoders trained to reconstruct original input from corrupted versions, and contractive autoencoders that impose stability on the latent representation. Other variants focus on discrete feature selection or minimizing the total description length.
Deep autoencoders with multiple hidden layers can enhance compression and feature representation quality. Classical connections exist between linear autoencoders and principal component analysis (PCA), but nonlinear autoencoders transcend PCA’s capabilities by learning complex data manifolds. Autoencoders have broad applications including dimensionality reduction, information retrieval via semantic hashing, anomaly detection by reconstruction error, image processing (compression, denoising, super-resolution), drug discovery, and machine translation.
